gap: No result ChatGPT got states what the under-$300 picks deliver at the AC outlet when one named tester measures them the same way: The Technology Man got 231 Wh from the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 (80% of 288 Wh) and 439 Wh from the EcoFlow River 2 Max at about 200 W (86% of 512 Wh), falling to 391 Wh (76%) near its 500 W limit. No named reviewer or lab has published a capacity measurement for ChatGPT's own pick, the Segway Lumina 500, or for the Pecron E500LFP.
standout_why: Compared against the cited Nineteen Lab page and the two uncited under-$300 roundups, portablepowerrank.com and powerstationpicks.net. Nineteen Lab says 'We have not bench-tested these units' and gets usable Wh by formula (rated × 0.85: 435 Wh for the River 2 Max, 245 Wh for the Elite 30 V2). powerstationpicks.net says 'We have not used these units' and names no tester. portablepowerrank.com carries one measured figure, OutdoorGearLab's 230 Wh for the Anker SOLIX C300, so rivals hold a small part of the angle. None has a measured figure for the Elite 30 V2, River 2 Max or Lumina 500, any inverter-on idle drain, or a measured recharge time or UPS switchover. ChatGPT's answer also used an assumed 85% and said 'not tested runtimes'.
decides: It confirms the split in the desk notes and sharpens it. On measured energy the River 2 Max gives about 1.9× the Elite 30 V2 (439 Wh vs 231 Wh at the AC outlet, same tester), so it wins capacity per dollar if its store price is still under $300; I could not read that price today. The Elite 30 V2 ($289.99 on BLUETTI's store today) wins the output, charging and UPS segment with measured figures: full in 51 minutes, switchover under 10 ms on an oscilloscope, almost 240 W from the two USB-C ports together. Two measured cautions belong on its row: 80% AC efficiency, which the tester called 'a little below average', and about 19 W of drain with the inverter on and Eco mode off, which emptied 81% of the battery in 12 hours with nothing plugged in. The Segway Lumina 500 can be listed on Segway's stated specs only; no named measurement backs its 512 Wh.

findings.label: Usable AC capacity, measured by The Technology Man (Gidon)
findings.value: 231 Wh, about 80% of the 288 Wh rating
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Power Station Is Better Than I Expected (The Technology Man)
findings.note: Review published 2025-12-23. Constant AC load: 'I measured 231 Wh, giving an efficiency of around 80%, which is a little below average.' 231 / 288 = 80.2%. Nineteen Lab's formula figure for this unit is 245 Wh.

findings.label: Usable DC capacity, measured by The Technology Man
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Power Station Is Better Than I Expected (The Technology Man)
findings.note: 'Running the same test on DC, I measured 244 Wh, or around 85% efficiency.'

findings.label: No-load drain with AC on and Eco mode off, measured by The Technology Man
findings.value: about 19 W (100% to 19% in 12 hours); DC output on: about 11 W (down to 24% in 20 hours)
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Power Station Is Better Than I Expected (The Technology Man)
findings.note: 'around 19 W just to keep the inverter running'. Arithmetic: 81% × 288 Wh = 233 Wh over 12 h = 19.4 W. BLUETTI's own '4.5W standby' is a different state from inverter-on idle, so the two figures do not contradict each other. The tester's unit was probably the UK 230 V version (the review prices it in £); the US 120 V unit may differ.

findings.label: Wall recharge in Turbo mode, measured by The Technology Man
findings.value: 80% in about 40 minutes; full in 51 minutes; up to 380 W input
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Power Station Is Better Than I Expected (The Technology Man)
findings.note: BLUETTI claims 80% in 45 minutes. Turbo has to be selected in the app. 'a full charge took just 51 minutes.'

findings.label: UPS switchover and output limits, measured by The Technology Man
findings.value: under 10 ms on an oscilloscope; no more than 600 W real power in Power Lifting; both USB-C ports together almost 240 W
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Power Station Is Better Than I Expected (The Technology Man)
findings.note: 'I also measured the transfer time with an oscilloscope and confirmed it was under 10 ms, as specified.' A 450 W air duster with a roughly 2,300 W start-up surge (clamp meter) overloaded the unit. Fan noise was not measured in dB: 'I couldn't hear the fans over normal room noise.' Weight 4.3 kg.

findings.label: BLUETTI US store price today (station alone)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Portable Power Station | 600W 288Wh (Blush Pink)

The listing text gives '4.5W standby', '<30dB' and 80% in 45 minutes (maker claims). I did not read ship dates for the grey colours. 231 Wh measured / $289.99 = 0.80 measured Wh per dollar.

findings.label: Second measurement: energy delivered and wall energy to refill, StorageReview (Jordan Ranous)
findings.value: 410 Wh out (about 80% of 512 Wh); 581 Wh from the wall for 2% to 100% in just under 1 hour at about 615 W
findings.note: Published 2022-10-25. 'finally powering off after putting out 410 watt hours'; 'consistently drawing 615 watts'. Round trip is my arithmetic: 410 / 581 = 71%. The discharge load is not stated.

findings.label: Observed behaviour, Dirt Wheels Magazine staff (app readings, not an independent capacity test)
findings.value: a 1,500 W heat gun on R-Drive spiked to 750 W, then settled at 599 W; four minutes of it took the app from 389 Wh to 337 Wh
findings.source_title: Segway Lumina 500 Portable Power Station - Product Evaluation (Dirt Wheels Magazine)
findings.note: Published 2025-10-17. All Wh figures are the unit's own app display, so they do not verify the 512 Wh rating. A 91-100 W compressor load for 30 minutes took the display from 512 Wh to 455 Wh. The magazine listed the price as $349.99 at the time. Recharge (1.2 h) and weight (15.9 lb) in the article are Segway's figures.

findings.label: Battery Skills review (Bernard Ryan): claims a capacity test but prints no result
findings.value: no measured Wh, efficiency, idle draw or dB figure on the page
findings.note: Dated 2025-09-15. It says 'We meticulously measured actual output capacity versus its rated 512Wh' but gives no number, and its FAQ assumes 'roughly 85% efficiency'. Its solar recharge times contradict each other. Not usable as a measurement.

findings.label: Usable AC capacity, measured by OutdoorGearLab (RJ Spurrier, Kenji Mowrey, Sentry Kelly)
findings.value: 230 Wh, 80% of the 288 Wh rating; 0-100% wall charge 1.1 h; 9.1 lb
findings.note: Page updated 2026-07-23. Method: a set AC load on a light-bar jig and bulb bank, capacity taken as usable AC output. This is the one measured figure a rival (portablepowerrank.com) already carries. OutdoorGearLab lists it at $429 list; the desk lead is $329.98, over the line. The page's tables disagree with each other on some other models.

findings.label: Usable AC capacity, measured by OutdoorGearLab
findings.value: 260 Wh, 89% of the 293 Wh rating; 0-100% wall charge 4.0 h; 7.1 lb
findings.note: OutdoorGearLab gives $289 list and 300 W max AC. This is the older Explorer 300, not the 300 v2. A 4-hour recharge is its weak point against the 51-minute Elite 30 V2.

findings.label: UPS switchover, measured by StorageReview (Dylan Dougherty)
findings.source_title: EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus Review: Compact Power Station with 600W Output & UPS Support (StorageReview)
findings.note: Published 2025-02-12: 'we measured a transfer time of 9ms.' The same review's discharge figure (0.43 kWh) exceeds the 286 Wh rating and is not usable as a capacity measurement. portablepowerrank.com lists this model as discontinued at $299; I did not read its price.

findings.label: What the cited rival and ChatGPT use instead of measurements
findings.value: an assumed 85%: 435 Wh for a 512 Wh unit, 245 Wh for a 288 Wh unit
findings.source_title: Best Portable Power Stations Under $300 (2026): Honest Tier Picks | Nineteen Lab
findings.note: 'We have not bench-tested these units — every number here comes from manufacturer specs and owner reports.' 'Runtime is watt-hours x 0.85 / watts.' Measured results span 76-86% for the River 2 Max depending on load and 80% for the Elite 30 V2 and Anker C300, so the flat 85% overstates the two 288 Wh units by about 14 Wh.
